# Wartime repression of Surrealism in Japan

Wartime repression of Surrealism in Japan refers to the police surveillance, censorship, arrests, interrogations, confiscation of works, renaming of groups, and other pressures that curtailed Surrealist activity in Japan in the late 1930s and early 1940s. The topic concerns the wartime conditions under which Surrealist writers, painters, critics, editors, and photographers worked, rather than the broader artistic history of Surrealism in Japan. Japanese Surrealism did not operate through a single national organization; it circulated through poetry journals, painting associations, exhibitions, criticism, and photography circles, which made the effects of wartime control uneven and dispersed. The best-known incident was the 1941 detention of Fukuzawa Ichirō and Shūzō Takiguchi, but wartime pressure also affected magazines, exhibitions, painting associations, poetry circles, and photography groups, including the Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde and the Surrealist journal Yoru no Funsui.
Background and political context
Surrealism in Japan developed through poetry, painting, photography, criticism, and small-scale publishing rather than through a single national organization. This dispersed structure shaped the way wartime pressure was felt: police attention and self-restraint could affect journals, exhibitions, associations, individual artists, and regional photography circles rather than one central group.
The political background was the tightening climate created by the Peace Preservation Law and the Special Higher Police. Stojković links the absence of a unified Surrealist centre in Japan to this legal and policing environment, under which organized opposition to state policy had been made illegal and public identification with suspect movements could invite surveillance or prosecution.
Publishing, exhibitions, and police scrutiny
Wartime pressure on Surrealism in Japan was not limited to a single prohibition or a single arrest. It worked through several overlapping forms: police suspicion of Surrealism's possible connection with communism, the interrogation or detention of individual figures, the confiscation of works and records, the closing or redirection of magazines, the self-restraint of artists' associations, and the adoption of safer names and critical terms. The 1990 Nagoya City Art Museum catalogue treated poetry journals, painting groups, exhibition catalogues, and photographic activity as connected parts of the prewar movement, while also placing wartime arrests and ideological pressure within the same historical sequence.
Because the movement was dispersed across writers, painters, critics, and photographers, the pressure did not appear only in formal legal action. Stojković describes Surrealist photography in 1930s Japan as a set of practices linked by magazines, exhibitions, critics, and local groups rather than by a single organization. As the decade progressed, that dispersed structure became vulnerable through police attention, changes in terminology, and the narrowing of public activity around journals, exhibitions, and associations.
The 1941 arrests of Fukuzawa and Takiguchi
The best-known wartime incident was the detention of Fukuzawa Ichirō and Shūzō Takiguchi in April 1941. The 1990 Nagoya City Art Museum chronology records their arrest and detention in the same year as the Bijutsu Bunka Association's declaration "Kokumin bijutsu no sōsei" and the detention of poets associated with Lien, placing the arrests within a wider wartime tightening around Surrealist and avant-garde circles.
In an essay on the wartime transformation of the Bijutsu Bunka Association, Ozaki Masato argues that the arrests of Takiguchi and Fukuzawa, which took place just before the association's second exhibition, also served as an effective warning to the wider avant-garde. He describes the association's subsequent declarations of loyalty and accommodation to wartime themes as part of a process of self-limitation and "self-extinction".
The pressure also extended to Nagoya. The painter Tetsu Okada, who had taken part in the Nagoya Avant-Garde Club and joined the Bijutsu Bunka Association in 1939, was searched by the Special Higher Police in 1941; the Kiyosu City Haruhi Museum of Art states that almost all of the works in his studio were confiscated. Sanshin Yoshikawa, another Nagoya painter associated with Surrealism and the Bijutsu Bunka Association, was detained by the Special Higher Police in 1941, had works and materials confiscated, and was released without indictment in 1942. The Toyohashi City Museum of Art and History also notes that a work Yoshikawa submitted to the second Bijutsu Bunka exhibition was removed as unsuitable to the times before he was detained by the Special Higher Police.
Yoru no Funsui and Nagoya photography circles
Nagoya offers a regional case of how police scrutiny and wartime caution affected Surrealist publishing and photography. A chronology in ''Japan's Modern Divide records that Kansuke Yamamoto was interrogated by the Thought Police in 1939 over Yoru no Funsui'' and was not permitted to continue publishing the journal in the same form. It also records that the Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde changed its name in November 1939 to the Nagoya Photography Culture Association in order to avoid attracting police attention, moved in a more conservative direction, and dissolved in 1941.
The Nagoya example also shows that repression did not immediately end Surrealist practice. Stojković notes that some of Yamamoto's photographs made after his separation from the Nagoya club rank among the strongest examples of Surrealist photography produced in Japan during the decade, including works published in Kōkaku in 1940. The case therefore shows both the contraction of public activity and the persistence of Surrealist photographic work under increasingly difficult conditions.
Renaming, self-restraint, and wartime adaptation
One response to the political climate was a change in terminology. Stojković argues that photographers negotiated their public position through critical rubrics such as "new", "avant-garde", and "plastic" photography, and that the discourse of zōkei shashin, or "plastic photography", helped make continued work possible even as the cultural field entered what she describes as its final stage of oppression in the 1930s.
The shift was visible in photography groups. The Avant-Garde Photography Association renamed itself the Experimental Photo Group, while the Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde became the Nagoya Photography Culture Association. The term zōkei, or "creating form", offered a more neutral alternative to the foreign and politically suspect terms "avant-garde" and "Surrealism". These changes did not always follow a direct police ban. In the Nagoya case, the change of name was followed by internal disagreement, a turn by some members toward cultural cooperation and national service, and the apparent end of the group's activities around 1941.
Aftermath and reassessment
The wartime curtailment of Surrealist activity contributed to the fragmentation of the movement before it could develop further. Stojković notes that there was no single postwar channel through which the achievements of Surrealist photography in the 1930s could be carried forward, not least because magazines had ceased publication, works had been lost, and postwar debates favored other tendencies.
Later scholarship and exhibitions have increasingly reconstructed this history. Munro identifies the 1990 Nagoya exhibition ''Japan's Surrealism 1925-1945'' as a major moment in the reassessment of Japanese Surrealism, while later museum catalogues and monographs have treated wartime pressure, regional networks, and Surrealist photography as central to understanding the movement in Japan.
